root.name: Philidor Defense: Exchange Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4

sources.title: Philidor Defense Adviser, Quiz & Replay Lab
Search snippet: Philidor Defense Guide / 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 Be7 plans

overview: After 3.d4 exd4 White recaptures (4.Nxd4 is the main line; Morphy's 4.Qxd4 is the alternative) and then has a space advantage and the more comfortable game. Black replies ...Nf6 and ...Be7, castles quickly and aims for a compact position (often with ...Nbd7 or ...c5/...c6 later) with king safety first, using ...d5 or ...c5 as freeing breaks. The structure is passive but not refuted: White cannot force a tactical win, but must prove an edge. Sources call it a sound, practical defence, an easy entry point for club players that is rarely used by top players because it concedes space; Aronian is mentioned as an occasional user. The Antoshin set-up (6.Be2) is a common White try.

white_ideas.idea: Take central space immediately with d4 and keep it; develop with Nc3, Be2 or Bc4, and castle either side, asking Black to prove the set-up.
Antoshin Variation: 5.Nc3 Be7 6.Be2 is a flexible, solid set-up; 6.Bc4 is the sharper alternative.
Morphy's 4.Qxd4 Nc6 gains time on the queen via Bb5 and queens-side castling lines; largely disappeared from modern practice.

black_ideas.idea: Develop harmoniously with ...Nf6, ...Be7 and rapid kingside castling (6...O-O), putting the second knight on d7 or c6; king safety first.
Prepare a well-timed central or queenside challenge with ...c6 or ...c5 (and ...d5), the freeing breaks that avoid long-term passivity.
Hanham-style set-up (...Nf6, ...Be7, ...Nbd7, ...O-O, ...c6) keeps a compact shell and waits for counterplay.

typical_structures.structure: After the d-pawns are traded: White e4 against Black d6, White with a space advantage and open d-file; Black develops behind the d6 pawn in a compact, cramped formation. (My own reading: it resembles an Open Sicilian/Scheveningen-type pawn structure.)

character.notes: Solid but passive. Wikipedia says the line is fundamentally sound but restrictive and leads to a position many regard as inferior despite having no tactical refutation. Chessworld calls it a sound and practical opening, especially at club level, where the Exchange route is a clear, structured, easy-to-understand game. Not a forcing or tactical line; risk of a quick loss is low but the long-term squeeze is the danger.

gambit.notes: The pawn on e5 is exchanged for the d-pawn; nothing is given.

soundness.notes: Sound. No tactical refutation exists; White enjoys a more comfortable position (more space) but cannot force an advantage. It is not considered dubious.

structure.notes: Central pawns have been exchanged (d4xd4) leaving White e4 against Black d6; the d-file is half-open and the game is a partly open position where White has the space and Black the compact structure. Not a locked centre.

approach.notes: A recognised defence to 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3, played by amateurs and occasionally by strong players. Wikipedia: seldom seen at top level (Aronian occasionally); it almost vanished from top-tier chess by WWI because other defences offer more active chances. Chessworld: stronger players use it as a practical weapon rather than a permanent mainstay. Not a system played against everything.

level.notes: Chessworld says it is suitable for beginners and intermediates who want a solid reply to 1.e4 without memorising much theory; plans are straightforward and king safety comes first. The hardest thing is judging when to break with ...c5/...d5 so as not to become too passive. Wikipedia says amateurs choose it because it is simpler and easier to understand than the complex heavily analysed alternatives.

sublines_that_differ.name: Morphy Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4 4. Qxd4
sublines_that_differ.how: White's queen comes out early; Black gains time with ...Nc6, giving a different queen-in-centre game rather than the usual Nxd4 structure.

sublines_that_differ.name: Antoshin Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 Be7 6. Be2
sublines_that_differ.how: The most flexible and solid White set-up; calmer than 6.Bc4 or the Be3/Qd2 attacking set-ups.

description.claim: The Exchange Variation is a solid and reliable, if somewhat passive, response to White's central push.
description.note: Wikipedia: solid but passive; Chessworld: sound and practical.

description.claim: By trading pawns immediately, Black avoids sharp tactical complications.
description.note: Chessworld calls the Exchange route the easiest entry point with a clear structure; there is no tactical refutation to worry about.

description.claim: Black aims for a resilient, cramped but defensible position.
description.note: Matches the sources' description of a restrictive but sound set-up.

common_plans.claim: White uses the space advantage to build a kingside attack, often with Be3, Qd2 and O-O-O.
common_plans.note: Space advantage is stated; I found no source that mentions the Be3/Qd2/O-O-O set-up against this line.

common_plans.claim: Black develops solidly with ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O and challenges White's centre with ...c5.
Black seeks to trade pieces to relieve the cramped position.
common_plans.note: No source mentions piece trades as a plan; it is plausible given the cramped position.

common_plans.claim: White maintains central control and piece activity, preventing Black's freeing breaks.
common_plans.note: Generic, but consistent with White asking Black to prove the set-up.

common_plans.claim: Black defends resiliently and aims for a favourable, often simplified, endgame.
common_plans.note: Resilience is supported, but no source mentions a favourable endgame as a Black goal.
